the comet assay is not suitable as a predictor of patient radiosensitivity and that the gamma-HAX assay is only a suitable predictor of patient radiosensitivities if the p53 status of the cells is known.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the neutral comet assay is not a reliable measure of radiosensitivity in human fibroblast strains, and the gamma-H2A X assay should be used with caution in the absence of knowledge of the p53 status.
the neutral comet assay, which measures unrejoined DSB, and the gamma-H2X assay, which measures the kinetics of DSB rejoining, are useful in the evaluation of the radiosensitivity of human cells.
the neutral comet assay and the gamma-H2X assay are complementary and should be used together in the assessment of clinical radiosensitivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of the gamma-H2X assay as a predictor of clinical radiosensitivity requires knowledge of the cells tested and that the use of this parameter in the absence of such information is not advisable.

the neutral comet and clonogenic assays are complementary in terms of the information they provide about radiosensitivity, and that both assays should be performed to fully evaluate the radiosensitivity of human fibroblast cells.

, for the prediction of radiosensitivity in patients, the p53 status must be known and taken into account when evaluating the DSB rejoining capability of fibroblasts by means of the neutral comet and/or gamma-H2AX assay.
